• C's other neighbour (besides A) must be E, so E sits at position 3 (C's neighbours are positions 1 and 3; position 1 is A, so E is at 3).

 

• Remaining positions {4, 6} are for D and G. B's neighbours are positions 6 and 1(A); since G cannot be B's neighbour, G ≠ position 6, so G = 4 and D = 6.

 

• Final arrangement (positions 0–6): 0=B, 1=A, 2=C, 3=E, 4=G, 5=F, 6=D.

 

• Counting from the left of D (position 6), moving clockwise: 6→0(B)→1(A)→2(C)→3(E). The people between D and E in this direction are B, A, C = 3 people.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option A.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• In circular seating with people facing the centre, 'right' corresponds to moving anticlockwise and 'left' to moving clockwise around the standard (clockwise-numbered) circle — fix this convention first and stick to it throughout to avoid direction errors.

 

NOTE

 

• Always place the person mentioned in the most clues (here B, referenced by 'second to the right of B' and 'not neighbour of B') at a fixed reference point first, to anchor the rest of the arrangement.

question:
Select the set in which the numbers are related in the same way as are the numbers of the following sets.

(NOTE: Operations should be performed on the whole numbers, without breaking down the numbers into their constituent digits. E.g. 13 – Operations on 13 such as adding to/subtracting from/multiplying with 13 can be performed. Breaking down 13 into 1 and 3 and then performing mathematical operations on 1 and 3 is not allowed.)

 

(22, 66, 61)

(35, 105, 100)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. (14, 42, 37).

 

GIVEN

 

• (22, 66, 61) and (35, 105, 100) follow a common pattern.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Check: 22 × 3 = 66 (matches 2nd number); 66 − 5 = 61 (matches 3rd number).

 

• Verify with the second set: 35 × 3 = 105 (matches); 105 − 5 = 100 (matches).

 

• Pattern confirmed: 2nd number = 1st × 3; 3rd number = 2nd number − 5.

 

• Testing Option B (14, 42, 37): 14 × 3 = 42 ✓; 42 − 5 = 37 ✓. Fully matches!

 

• Quick check of others: Option A (41,123,117): 41×3=123 ✓ but 123−5=118≠117 ✗. Option C (74,222,216): 74×3=222 ✓ but 222−5=217≠216 ✗. Option D (85,255,249): 85×3=255 ✓ but 255−5=250≠249 ✗.

 

• Only Option B satisfies both steps of the pattern exactly.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Once you find a plausible two-step rule (×3, then −5), verify it against BOTH given example sets before testing options — this avoids being misled by a rule that fits only one example by coincidence.

 

NOTE

 

• In this type of question, the correct option is often the only one where errors don't creep in exactly at the last step — always carry out both steps of the rule fully for every option instead of stopping after the first matching step.

question:
If 'A' stands for '÷', 'B' stands for '×', 'C' stands for '+' and 'D' stands for '-', what will come in place of the question mark '?' in the following equation?

 

25 C 15 A 3 D 9 B 3 = ?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. 3.

 

GIVEN

 

• A=÷, B=×, C=+, D=−. Equation: 25 C 15 A 3 D 9 B 3 = ?

 

SOLUTION

 

• Substitute the symbols: 25 + 15 ÷ 3 − 9 × 3 = ?

 

• Apply BODMAS: 15 ÷ 3 = 5; 9 × 3 = 27.

 

• 25 + 5 − 27 = 30 − 27 = 3.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• First substitute all letters with their actual symbols to rewrite the full equation, THEN apply BODMAS — never try to calculate while the letters are still unsubstituted, as it's easy to apply the wrong order of operations.

 

NOTE

 

• Always perform division and multiplication before addition and subtraction, exactly as in a normal arithmetic expression, once the substitution is done.

question:
What will come in place of the question mark (?) in the following equation, if '+' and '÷' are interchanged and '−' and '×' are interchanged?

 

850 + 34 × 15 − 12 ÷ 400 = ?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. 245.

 

GIVEN

 

• Original: 850 + 34 × 15 − 12 ÷ 400. Swap: '+' ↔ '÷', '−' ↔ '×'.

 

SOLUTION

 

• After swapping, the expression becomes: 850 ÷ 34 − 15 × 12 + 400.

 

• Apply BODMAS: 850 ÷ 34 = 25; 15 × 12 = 180.

 

• 25 − 180 + 400 = −155 + 400 = 245.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Rewrite the entire expression with the new (swapped) symbols FIRST, then solve using standard BODMAS — trying to swap operations mentally while calculating leads to errors.

 

NOTE

 

• Remember both swaps happen simultaneously — a common mistake is swapping only one pair of operators and forgetting the other.

question:
What should come in place of the question mark (?) in the given series?

 

510 511 500 501 491 492 ?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option D i.e. 483.

 

GIVEN

 

• 510, 511, 500, 501, 491, 492, ?

 

SOLUTION

 

• Find the differences between consecutive terms: 511−510=+1; 500−511=−11; 501−500=+1; 491−501=−10; 492−491=+1; ?−492=−9 (pattern continues: +1, −11, +1, −10, +1, −9...).

 

• The '+1' steps alternate with decreasing-magnitude negative steps: −11, −10, −9 (increasing by 1 each time).

 

• Missing term = 492 − 9 = 483.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option D.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• This is a paired/alternating series — group the terms in pairs (510,511), (500,501), (491,492), (483,...) and notice each pair's first term drops by 11, then 10, then 9 from the previous pair's first term — the gap shrinks by 1 each time.

 

NOTE

 

• Whenever a series doesn't follow a single simple pattern, check if it's actually TWO interleaved patterns (alternating +1 with a shrinking negative step, as here).

question:

solution_text:

• 36, 41, 51, 66, 86, ?

 

SOLUTION

• The differences themselves increase by 5 each time: 5, 10, 15, 20, so the next difference = 25.

 

• Missing term = 86 + 25 = 111.

NOTE

 

• This is a classic 'second-order arithmetic' series (differences of differences are constant) — always check the differences-of-differences when the first-level differences aren't constant.

question:
Read the given statements and conclusions carefully. Assuming that the information given in the statements is true, even if it appears to be at variance with commonly known facts, decide which of the given conclusion(s) logically follow(s) from the statements.

 

Statements:

All flowers are plants.

Some plants are trees.

 

Conclusions:

(I) Some trees are flowers.

(II) All flowers are trees.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. Neither conclusion (I) nor (II) follows.

 

GIVEN

 

• All flowers are plants (Flowers ⊆ Plants). Some plants are trees (Plants ∩ Trees exists, but not necessarily including the Flowers subset).

 

SOLUTION

 

• Since flowers form only a portion (possibly a small one) of all plants, and only 'some' plants overlap with trees, there is no guarantee that this 'some' overlap includes any flowers at all.

 

• Conclusion (I): Some trees are flowers — this requires that the tree-plant overlap intersects the flower subset, which is not guaranteed by the given statements — does not follow.

 

• Conclusion (II): All flowers are trees — this is an even stronger claim and is clearly not guaranteed, since 'some plants are trees' does not mean 'all plants (including all flowers) are trees' — does not follow.

 

• Since neither conclusion is necessarily true in every valid diagram, the correct answer is Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Whenever the link between two classes passes through a 'some' relationship, always test whether you can draw AT LEAST ONE valid diagram where the conclusion is false — if you can, the conclusion doesn't follow, regardless of how 'likely' it looks intuitively.

 

NOTE

 

• This is a very standard trap: 'All A are B, Some B are C' does NOT allow any conclusion connecting A and C — memorise this as a reliable checkpoint.

question:

How many such odd numbers are there (from left to right) which are immediately followed by an even number?

SOLUTION

• Two odd numbers (9 and 3) are immediately followed by an even number.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Underline all odd numbers first, then just glance at the term immediately to the right of each underlined number to check if it's even — a quick systematic left-to-right scan avoids missing any occurrence.

 

NOTE

 

• The very last term in the series can never 'qualify' for a 'followed by' condition since it has no term after it — always exclude it from consideration.

question: HN 9 is related to LK -3 in a certain way. In the same way, NY 4 is related to RV -8. To which of the given options is OU 13 related, following the same logic?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. SR 1.

 

GIVEN

 

• HN9 → LK−3; NY4 → RV−8; find the match for OU13.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Letter shift for both letters: H(8)→L(12) is +4; N(14)→K(11) is −3. Check with the second pair: N(14)→R(18) is +4; Y(25)→V(22) is −3. Both pairs show the SAME letter shifts (+4 for the first letter, −3 for the second letter) — pattern confirmed.

 

• Number transformation: 9 → −3 (a change of −12); 4 → −8 (a change of −12). So the rule for the number is: subtract 12.

 

• Apply to OU13: O(15)+4 = 19 = S; U(21)−3 = 18 = R. Number: 13 − 12 = 1.

 

• Result = SR 1.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Split the analogy into three independent parts (1st letter, 2nd letter, number) and find each one's fixed transformation rule using BOTH given examples before applying it to the new term — this avoids being misled by a rule that fits only one example.

 

NOTE

 

• The letter shifts here are OPPOSITE in sign (+4 and −3) — always check each letter position separately rather than assuming a single uniform shift applies to both letters.

question: Seven people B, C, D, I, J, K and L are sitting in a straight line facing north. No one sits to the left of K. Only four people sit between K and J. L sits second to the left of J. D sits to the immediate left of B. C is not an immediate neighbour of L. How many people sit between L and C?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. Two.

 

GIVEN

 

• 7 people in a row facing north. K is at the extreme left (no one to K's left). Exactly 4 people sit between K and J. L is 2nd to the left of J. D is immediately left of B. C is not an immediate neighbour of L.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Number the positions 1 to 7 from the left. K = position 1 (nobody to its left).

 

• 4 people between K(1) and J means J is at position 1 + 4 + 1 = 6.

 

• L sits 2nd to the left of J(6): L = 6 − 2 = 4.

 

• D is immediately left of B: the only consecutive pair of positions left among {2, 3, 5, 7} is (2, 3), so D = 2, B = 3.

 

• Remaining positions {5, 7} are for C and I. C cannot be an immediate neighbour of L(4); position 5 IS a neighbour of position 4, so C cannot be at 5 — hence C = 7 and I = 5.

 

• Final arrangement: 1=K, 2=D, 3=B, 4=L, 5=I, 6=J, 7=C.

 

• People between L(4) and C(7): positions 5 and 6 = I and J = 2 people.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Fix the person defined by an extreme/absolute clue first (here K, 'no one to the left'), then work through relative clues (distance from K, position relative to J, etc.) step by step to pin down each remaining seat.

 

NOTE

 

• Where multiple positions remain open, use exclusion clues (like 'C is not an immediate neighbour of L') last, after narrowing down candidates via the more restrictive clues.

question: Seven people, A, B, C, D, E, F and G, are sitting in a row, facing north. Only six people sit to the right of C. Only four people sit to the left of B. D sits to the left of A but right of B. F sits second to the right of G. How many people sit to the right of E?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option A i.e. Four.

 

GIVEN

 

• 7 people in a row facing north. Only 6 people sit to the right of C. Only 4 people sit to the left of B. D sits left of A but right of B. F sits 2nd to the right of G.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Number positions 1 to 7 from the left. 'Only 6 to the right of C' means C is at position 1 (leftmost).

 

• 'Only 4 to the left of B' means B is at position 5 (positions 1-4 are to its left).

 

• D sits right of B(5) and left of A: both D and A must be among the remaining positions {6, 7} with D < A, so D = 6, A = 7.

 

• Remaining positions {2, 3, 4} are for E, F, G. F is 2nd to the right of G: G and F must be 2 apart within {2,3,4}, so G = 2, F = 4, leaving E = 3.

 

• Final arrangement: 1=C, 2=G, 3=E, 4=F, 5=B, 6=D, 7=A.

 

• People to the right of E(3): positions 4, 5, 6, 7 = F, B, D, A = 4 people.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option A.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• 'Only N people sit to the right/left of X' directly fixes X's absolute position (from that end) in a row of known total size — always convert such clues into a fixed position first before handling relative clues.

 

NOTE

 

• After fixing extreme-position clues, resolve 'between' clues (like D between B and A) using the remaining free positions, checking the direction (right of B, left of A) carefully.

question:
Based on the English alphabetical order, three of the following four letter-cluster pairs are alike in a certain way and thus form a group. Which letter-cluster pair DOES NOT belong to that group?

(Note: The odd one out is not based on the number of consonants/vowels or their position in the letter-cluster.)
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option C i.e. HM-ZW.

 

GIVEN

 

• SY-KH, WC-OL, HM-ZW, BH-TQ.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Check the letter-position shift from the first letter to the corresponding letter of the second cluster (1st→1st and 2nd→2nd), using mod-26 arithmetic.

 

• SY-KH: S(19)→K(11) is −8; Y(25)→H(8) is +9 (mod 26, since 25+9=34, 34−26=8).

 

• WC-OL: W(23)→O(15) is −8; C(3)→L(12) is +9.

 

• BH-TQ: B(2)→T(20) is −8 (mod 26, since 2−8=−6, −6+26=20); H(8)→Q(17) is +9.

 

• These three all follow the SAME pattern: first letter shifts −8, second letter shifts +9.

 

• HM-ZW: H(8)→Z(26) is −8 (mod 26, 8−8=0≡26=Z ✓ matches), but M(13)→W(23) is +10, NOT +9 — this breaks the pattern.

 

• Since HM-ZW does not follow the common −8/+9 rule, it is the odd one out.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Compute the shift for the FIRST letter of each pair first — if all four match on that shift, then check the second letter's shift to isolate the outlier (as here, where all four match on −8 for the first letter, but only HM-ZW fails on the second letter's shift).

 

NOTE

 

• Always use modular (wraparound) arithmetic for alphabet shifts, e.g. treating a result of 0 as 26 (Z), since letter sequences wrap around from Z back to A.

question:
In the following triads, each group of letters is related to the subsequent one following a certain logic. Select from the given options, the one which follows the same logic.

WASH - HSWA - WSAH

CORE - ERCO - CROE
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option D i.e. INKS - SKIN - IKNS.

 

GIVEN

 

• WASH→HSWA→WSAH and CORE→ERCO→CROE both follow the same letter-rearrangement logic.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Step 1 (word1→word2): WASH (W₁A₂S₃H₄) → HSWA takes letters from positions [4,3,1,2] i.e. H(4th),S(3rd),W(1st),A(2nd). Check with CORE→ERCO: positions [4,3,1,2] → E(4th),R(3rd),C(1st),O(2nd) = ERCO ✓. Pattern for step 1 confirmed: new order = positions [4,3,1,2].

 

• Step 2 (word2→word3): HSWA (H₁S₂W₃A₄) → WSAH takes positions [3,2,4,1] i.e. W(3rd),S(2nd),A(4th),H(1st) = WSAH ✓. Check with ERCO→CROE: positions [3,2,4,1] → C(3rd),R(2nd),O(4th),E(1st) = CROE ✓. Pattern for step 2 confirmed: new order = positions [3,2,4,1].

 

• Test Option D: INKS (I₁N₂K₃S₄) → apply [4,3,1,2]: S(4th),K(3rd),I(1st),N(2nd) = SKIN ✓ (matches given step 2 word).

 

• SKIN (S₁K₂I₃N₄) → apply [3,2,4,1]: I(3rd),K(2nd),N(4th),S(1st) = IKNS ✓ (matches given step 3 word).

 

• Both transformations match exactly for Option D.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option D.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Work out the positional-rearrangement rule as a numeric code (like [4,3,1,2] then [3,2,4,1]) using the given examples, then simply apply that same numeric code mechanically to each option — far faster and more reliable than re-deriving a fresh pattern for every option.

 

NOTE

 

• Once the rearrangement code is known, it must match BOTH transformation steps (word1→word2 AND word2→word3) for an option to be correct — checking only one step can give a false positive.

question: Yogesh ranked 34th from the top and 38th from the bottom in his class. How many students are there in his class?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option A i.e. 71.

 

GIVEN

 

• Yogesh's rank = 34th from the top, 38th from the bottom.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Total number of students = (Rank from top) + (Rank from bottom) − 1 = 34 + 38 − 1 = 71.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option A.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Memorise the standard formula: Total = (position from one end) + (position from the other end) − 1 — the '−1' accounts for the person being counted from both ends.

 

NOTE

 

• A common mistake is simply adding the two ranks (34+38=72) without subtracting 1 for the double-counted individual — always subtract 1.

question:

solution_text:

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

• When a term is missing near the start of the series, first establish the difference pattern from the KNOWN later terms, then extend that pattern backward to find the missing value.

 

NOTE

 

• Here the differences form their own arithmetic progression (8, 9, 10, 11, 12) — a classic 'second-order' series pattern.

question:
Based on the English alphabetical order, three of the following four letter-clusters are alike in a certain way and thus form a group. Which is the letter-cluster that DOES NOT belong to that group?

(Note: The odd one out is not based on the number of consonants/vowels or their position in the letter-cluster.)

question: In a certain code language, 'steak equal thing' is coded as 'wb vl yn' and 'thing yard house' is coded as 'vl za ha'. How is 'thing' coded in the given language?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option A i.e. vl.

 

GIVEN

 

• 'steak equal thing' → 'wb vl yn'.

 

• 'thing yard house' → 'vl za ha'.

 

SOLUTION

 

• Compare the two statements: the common word between them is 'thing'.

 

• The common code word between 'wb vl yn' and 'vl za ha' is 'vl'.

 

• Since 'thing' is the only word common to both English phrases, and 'vl' is the only code word common to both coded phrases, 'thing' must be coded as 'vl'.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option A.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Whenever a word repeats across two coded statements, its code must be the one code-word that also repeats across both coded outputs — simply find the common word and the common code, and match them.

 

NOTE

 

• This technique (finding common word ⇒ common code) is the fastest way to solve such coding questions without needing to decode every single word.

question:
Which of the following letter-number clusters will replace the question mark (?) in the given series to make it logically complete?

 

VDE97, BJK74, HPQ51, NVW28, ?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option B i.e. TBC5.

 

GIVEN

 

• VDE97, BJK74, HPQ51, NVW28, ?

 

SOLUTION

 

• Letter part: V(22)→B(2): +6 (mod 26, since 22+6=28, 28−26=2); D(4)→J(10): +6; E(5)→K(11): +6. All three letters shift by +6.

 

• Verify with next pair: B(2)+6=8=H; J(10)+6=16=P; K(11)+6=17=Q → gives HPQ ✓. And H(8)+6=14=N; P(16)+6=22=V; Q(17)+6=23=W → gives NVW ✓. Pattern confirmed.

 

• Apply +6 to NVW: N(14)+6=20=T; V(22)+6=28→28−26=2=B; W(23)+6=29→29−26=3=C. Letters = TBC.

 

• Number part: 97, 74, 51, 28, ?. Differences: 74−97=−23; 51−74=−23; 28−51=−23 (constant difference of −23).

 

• Next number = 28 − 23 = 5.

 

• Combined result: TBC5.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option B.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• Split the letter-number cluster into two independent tracks (letters and number) and solve each with its own simple pattern (+6 mod 26 for letters; −23 arithmetic progression for numbers) rather than trying to find one combined rule.

 

NOTE

 

• The number sequence here (97,74,51,28,5) is a straightforward arithmetic progression with common difference −23 — always check for simple AP patterns in the numeric part first.

question: In a certain code language, 'OVAL' is coded as '6729' and 'LEVO' is coded as '7946'. What is the code for 'E' in the given code language?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option A i.e. 4.

 

GIVEN

 

• OVAL → 6729 (so O=6, V=7, A=2, L=9, reading left to right).

 

• LEVO → 7946 (digits 7, 9, 4, 6, for letters L, E, V, O).

 

SOLUTION

 

• From OVAL, the codes for the letters O, V and L (which also appear in LEVO) are known: O=6, V=7, L=9.

 

• The code for LEVO is the digit-set {7, 9, 4, 6}. Removing the already-known codes for L, V and O (9, 7, 6) from this set leaves exactly one digit: 4.

 

• Since E is the only letter in LEVO whose code is not yet known, this leftover digit must be E's code.

 

• Code for E = 4.

 

• Therefore, the correct answer is: Option A.

 

SHORT TRICK

 

• When a new letter appears alongside letters whose codes you already know (from a previous coded word), find its code by elimination: remove the known digits from the new word's digit-set, and whatever digit remains belongs to the new letter.

 

NOTE

 

• This elimination method is especially useful when the exact left-to-right positional mapping isn't perfectly consistent between the two coded words — matching by known-letter/known-digit sets is more robust than assuming strict positional order.
